title: Clear statements and Spending Clause notice
shortTitle: Clear statements and Spending Clause notice
summary: A clear-statement rule requires sufficiently explicit statutory language before an interpretation can impose a specified kind of legal consequence.
notes:
The majority in Arlington treats federal funding as requiring clear notice to recipient states and school districts of the obligations attached to accepting funds. It concludes that attorneys’ fees as part of costs did not clearly notify recipients of liability for expert fees, and that the conference report could not supply what the text lacked.

Ginsburg agreed on the textual result but rejected the majority’s Spending Clause reasoning. The dissent emphasized purpose, the explicit report, and the enacted study of expenses. Katzmann’s broader criticism asks whether legislative drafters actually know judicial clear-statement conventions and whether changing those conventions disrupts expectations. The concept records the competing rationales rather than presenting the entire judgment as unanimous endorsement of a single canon.
